title: Western Powers Push to Refer Iran to UN Security Council as IAEA Warns of Nuclear Access Crisis
excerpt: The US, UK, France and Germany have drafted a resolution to send Iran's nuclear file to the Security Council for the first time in two decades, as the IAEA says it has lost knowledge of Iran's enriched uranium stocks.
body:
• The US, UK, France and Germany have submitted a draft resolution to the IAEA board to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for nuclear non-compliance
  • IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi says the agency has lost continuity of knowledge over Iran's enriched uranium stocks — including material enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade — since strikes on nuclear facilities in June 2025
  • Iran rejects the move, blaming access restrictions on the consequences of US and Israeli attacks on its nuclear sites
  • The standoff has implications for India's energy security, oil prices and the Chabahar port partnership

A New Escalation at the IAEA

The United States, Britain, France and Germany have submitted a draft resolution to the International Atomic Energy Agency's 35-member Board of Governors that would refer Iran to the UN Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

If adopted — and diplomats say it is likely to pass by a clear margin — it would be the first time in two decades that Iran's nuclear file has been sent to the Security Council, a body empowered to impose legally binding sanctions and asset freezes.

The resolution asks IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi to transmit the text, along with previous board decisions and his latest report, to both the Security Council and the UN General Assembly.

What the IAEA Is Saying

Grossi opened the quarterly board meeting on Monday with a blunt assessment. "It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge" over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to as much as 60% — close to the roughly 90% needed for a weapon — at facilities hit in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, he said.

"If Iran engages with us in a serious dialogue, if we can start getting access… I can guarantee to you that this will have very, very positive repercussions."

— Rafael Grossi, IAEA Director-General

Prior to the June 2025 strikes, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%. Since those strikes, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain. The agency halted inspections at affected sites on safety grounds in February due to renewed military strikes, and has since only inspected Iran's operating power plant at Bushehr.

Iran Pushes Back

Tehran has rejected the resolution and maintains its nuclear programme is peaceful. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei argued that restrictions facing inspectors were a direct consequence of the US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities.

"Whenever they run out of options, they turn to the agency and Grossi," Baghaei said at his weekly press conference. He warned that Iran would take "necessary measures" if Western powers pursued the resolution.

However, any punitive action by the Security Council remains unlikely. Iran's allies Russia and China hold veto power, making binding sanctions or asset freezes a remote prospect.

Why This Matters for India

The Iran nuclear standoff carries direct implications for India and its diaspora. India, the world's third-largest oil importer, has already faced the cost of Middle East instability through energy disruptions, higher import costs and inflation. While India weaned itself off Iranian crude imports following earlier US sanctions, any escalation around the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly a fifth of global oil passes — could spike prices for Indian consumers.

India also has strategic interests in Iran through the Chabahar port, its only deep-water oceanic port that provides India a maritime route to Central Asia bypassing Pakistan. US sanctions uncertainty has repeatedly complicated India's operations there.

More broadly, India has balanced its relationships carefully — defending ties with Russia despite Western pressure while maintaining working relationships with both Iran and the United States. The trajectory of this nuclear standoff could test that balancing act further.

What's Next

The IAEA board is expected to vote on the resolution later this week. Even if it passes, the practical impact depends on whether the Security Council takes further action — an unlikely prospect given the Russia-China veto. Meanwhile, the resolution risks complicating ongoing US-Iran talks aimed at extending their ceasefire and opening a path to broader negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme.
